3: I did not die, and I alive remained not; Think for thyself now, hast thou aught of wit, What I became, being of both deprived.
8: The Emperor of the kingdom dolorous From his mid-breast forth issued from the ice; And better with a giant I compare
13: Than do the giants with those arms of his; Consider now how great must be that whole, Which unto such a part conforms itself.
18: Were he as fair once, as he now is foul, And lifted up his brow against his Maker, Well may proceed from him all tribulation.
23: O, what a marvel it appeared to me, When I beheld three faces on his head! The one in front, and that vermilion was;
28: Two were the others, that were joined with this Above the middle part of either shoulder, And they were joined together at the crest;
33: And the right-hand one seemed ’twixt white and yellow; The left was such to look upon as those Who come from where the Nile falls valley-ward.
39: Underneath each came forth two mighty wings, Such as befitting were so great a bird; Sails of the sea I never saw so large.
44: No feathers had they, but as of a bat Their fashion was; and he was waving them, So that three winds proceeded forth therefrom.
49: Thereby Cocytus wholly was congealed. With six eyes did he weep, and down three chins Trickled the tear-drops and the bloody drivel.
55: At every mouth he with his teeth was crunching A sinner, in the manner of a brake, So that he three of them tormented thus.
59: To him in front the biting was as naught Unto the clawing, for sometimes the spine Utterly stripped of all the skin remained.
63: “That soul up there which has the greatest pain,” The Master said, “is Judas Iscariot; With head inside, he plies his legs without.
66: Of the two others, who head downward are, The one who hangs from the black jowl is Brutus; See how he writhes himself, and speaks no word.
69: And the other, who so stalwart seems, is Cassius. But night is reascending, and ’tis time That we depart, for we have seen the whole.”
74: As seemed him good, I clasped him round the neck, And he the vantage seized of time and place, And when the wings were opened wide apart,
79: He laid fast hold upon the shaggy sides; From fell to fell descended downward then Between the thick hair and the frozen crust.
84: When we were come to where the thigh revolves Exactly on the thickness of the haunch, The Guide, with labour and with hard-drawn breath,
89: Turned round his head where he had had his legs, And grappled to the hair, as one who mounts, So that to Hell I thought we were returning.
94: “Keep fast thy hold, for by such stairs as these,” The Master said, panting as one fatigued, “Must we perforce depart from so much evil.”
99: Then through the opening of a rock he issued, And down upon the margin seated me; Then tow’rds me he outstretched his wary step.
103: I lifted up mine eyes and thought to see Lucifer in the same way I had left him; And I beheld him upward hold his legs.
107: And if I then became disquieted, Let stolid people think who do not see What the point is beyond which I had passed.
111: “Rise up,” the Master said, “upon thy feet; The way is long, and difficult the road, And now the sun to middle-tierce returns.”
116: It was not any palace corridor There where we were, but dungeon natural, With floor uneven and unease of light.
120: “Ere from the abyss I tear myself away, My Master,” said I when I had arisen, “To draw me from an error speak a little;
124: Where is the ice? and how is this one fixed Thus upside down? and how in such short time From eve to morn has the sun made his transit?”
129: And he to me: “Thou still imaginest Thou art beyond the centre, where I grasped The hair of the fell worm, who mines the world.
133: That side thou wast, so long as I descended; When round I turned me, thou didst pass the point To which things heavy draw from every side,
138: And now beneath the hemisphere art come Opposite that which overhangs the vast Dry-land, and ’neath whose cope was put to death
143: The Man who without sin was born and lived. Thou hast thy feet upon the little sphere Which makes the other face of the Judecca.
145: Here it is morn when it is evening there; And he who with his hair a stairway made us Still fixed remaineth as he was before.
150: Upon this side he fell down out of heaven; And all the land, that whilom here emerged, For fear of him made of the sea a veil,
153: And came to our hemisphere; and peradventure To flee from him, what on this side appears Left the place vacant here, and back recoiled.”
157: A place there is below, from Beelzebub As far receding as the tomb extends, Which not by sight is known, but by the sound
158: Of a small rivulet, that there descendeth Through chasm within the stone, which it has gnawed With course that winds about and slightly falls.
159: The Guide and I into that hidden road Now entered, to return to the bright world; And without care of having any rest
161: We mounted up, he first and I the second, Till I beheld through a round aperture Some of the beauteous things that Heaven doth bear;
168: Thence we came forth to rebehold the stars.
